summary:
Zamfara State stands under Nigeria's national legal framework and, in addition, under its own Sharia criminal-law layer, which Zamfara itself introduced. Human Rights Watch's 2004 report on the extension of Sharia to criminal law records that Zamfara's governor was the first to move, promulgating the Sharia Establishment Law on 27 October 1999, in force 27 January 2000. By 2002 twelve northern states had adopted some form of Sharia into their criminal legislation, and those twelve remain the only states in Nigeria where Sharia courts hold jurisdiction to try criminal cases.

The Zamfara State Attorney-General and Commissioner for Justice at the time, Alh. Ahmed Bello Mahmud, set out the state's own account of the adoption at a seminar sponsored by the Jama'atu Nasril Islam on 6 July 2000. His account describes the enabling statute, the Sharia Courts (Administration of Justice and Certain Consequential Changes) Law 1999, enacted under section 6 of the 1999 Constitution, which created Sharia courts with criminal jurisdiction in Islamic law and made possible the codification of a Sharia Penal Code. Court administration passed to the Grand Kadi on 29 June 2000, alongside policy measures directed at prostitution and gambling.

The adoption process began with a committee appointed by Zamfara's governor in June 1999, mandated to study implementation of Sharia including the full scope of Islamic criminal law. By the end of 2000 eleven other northern states had followed. The codification of offences and punishments produced a penal-code architecture that the Sharia courts of all twelve states apply, a framework Zamfara pioneered across the northern bloc.
tangentialFactors:
Zamfara's first-mover status gives it a distinctive position within Nigeria: it is the origin point of the northern Sharia criminal-law wave, and the model it drafted was carried into eleven other state criminal codes within roughly eighteen months. A visitor in Zamfara is therefore in the jurisdiction where the framework was designed, not one that adopted it later under external pressure.

The twelve-state bloc shares a common architecture of codified offences and punishments applied through Sharia courts, so the criminal-law environment in Zamfara is not idiosyncratic to the state; the same structure operates across the northern states where Sharia courts have criminal jurisdiction.
localsOnly:
Zamfara residents are subject to the state's own Sharia criminal jurisdiction, established by the Sharia Establishment Law and administered through the Sharia Courts (Administration of Justice and Certain Consequential Changes) Law 1999. The codified Sharia Penal Code drafted under that framework is the instrument through which offences and punishments are applied in Zamfara's Sharia courts.

Court administration has been under the Grand Kadi since 29 June 2000. State policy under the adoption programme has targeted prostitution and gambling, indicating the categories of conduct that enforcement has prioritised alongside the codified offences.
outOfScopeNotes:
No Zamfara-specific arrest, prosecution or incident involving a trans or gender-nonconforming person appears in the sourced inventory; the state-level enforcement picture for such individuals is unresolved rather than documented as absent.

Whether the codified Sharia Penal Code drafted under the 1999 framework contains provisions addressing gender presentation, clothing or identity is not sourced here, and the practical interaction between that code and Nigeria's national statute in Zamfara's courts is likewise unresolved.

No visitor-facing official guidance specific to Zamfara was identified in the inventory; the assessment rests on the state's enabling legislation and the historical account of its adoption.
